Libya’s National Oil Corp Enters Insolvency, Disrupting Domestic Production and Exports

Libya’s oil and gas sector is facing renewed turbulence as National Oil Corp, the country’s flagship oil producer, has entered insolvency proceedings, industry sources confirmed on Wednesday. The development has sent shockwaves through the sector, with immediate effects on the company’s operations and uncertainty over the future of Libya’s energy exports.

The state-controlled National Oil Corp, which oversees the majority of Libya’s oil production, is currently undergoing court-supervised administration following a rapid deterioration in its financial position. According to documents seen by industry analysts, the company filed for insolvency late last week, citing mounting debts and a lack of access to international credit lines.

"National Oil Corp’s insolvency is a critical juncture for Libya’s oil industry," said Sami al-Darwish, an energy analyst based in Tripoli. "Production at several key fields has already been curtailed due to cash flow issues and difficulties in maintaining equipment."

Employees at the company’s Ras Lanuf and Zawiya facilities reported that maintenance work had been suspended and several drilling operations put on hold. "We haven’t received wages for two months," said an engineer at one of the affected sites, who asked not to be named. "There are real concerns about safety and the ability to keep operations running."

Market observers estimate that overall production has declined by approximately 18% since the beginning of June, with exports from major ports down sharply. The Libyan Oil Workers’ Union warned that further disruptions were likely if the insolvency process drags on. "Our members are worried about job security and the future of the industry," said union spokesperson Hatem al-Maghrabi. "We urge the authorities to prioritize a solution to safeguard employees and national assets."

The Libyan Energy Chamber, a trade body representing local service providers, echoed concerns about the wider impact on the economy. "National Oil Corp’s troubles are already affecting contractors and suppliers across the country," said chairwoman Fadila Omar. "Without swift intervention, the effects could ripple through the entire supply chain."

While the government has not yet announced a formal rescue package, an emergency meeting of sector officials was convened on Tuesday evening. "All options are being considered to stabilize operations and protect Libya’s vital oil revenues," said a senior official, declining to be identified.

The insolvency process is ongoing, with stakeholders awaiting clarity on the company’s restructuring and the fate of Libya’s critical oil exports.
